[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | People have long disagreed over whether jinn exist: most philosophers apparently deny them, while most religious communities and many ancient philosophers affirm them.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من الناس | reports | This proposal calls the helper an angel and its influence inspiration when the soul is good, but a devil and whispering when it is evil.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن سينا | reports | Ibn Sīnā defines jinn as an airy animal able to assume different forms; Rāzī reads his calling this a definition of the name as evidence he is explaining a term, not affirming an external entity.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحاب الروحانيات | reports | Many ancient philosophers and spiritualists affirm jinn and call them lower spirits; they say these respond faster but are weaker than celestial spirits, which respond more slowly but are stronger.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المثبتين | reports | One group of those affirming jinn says they are independent substances, neither bodies nor states inhering in bodies; sharing a negation does not make them equal to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المثبتين | reports | These proponents say the immaterial beings differ in essence and moral kind: some are good or noble, others evil or base, and only God knows their kinds and number.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المثبتين | reports | They maintain that immaterial jinn can know reported events, hear, see, and perform particular deeds; some kinds can perform feats beyond human power.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المثبتين | reports | The proponents analogize jinn attachment to bodies with the human soul’s attachment through fine vaporous spirits formed from the blood’s finest parts in the left side of the heart.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المثبتين | reports | On this account, a jinn first attaches to a portion of air, then gains influence over a dense body as that air passes through it.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p131#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من الناس | reports | Another proposal identifies jinn with departed human souls, which gain strength and insight after death and may attach to a new, similar body to assist its soul.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Dividing bodies into subtle and dense does not prove that all bodies share a common essence, just as dividing accidents into quality and quantity does not establish shared essential properties.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A subtle airy body could differ essentially from other air, with its nature entailing distinctive knowledge and extraordinary power; this makes jinn and their ability to assume forms plausible.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأشعري وجمهور أتباعه | prefers | Al-Ashʿarī and most followers deny that bodily structure is a condition for life.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Their argument is that one life cannot inhere simultaneously in many substrates; if each equal part had its own life, dependence between the parts would create a circle, so an individual part can live independently.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites argue that structure is necessary because life disappears when the structure breaks down and remains while it stays intact.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī rejects that induction as proof of necessity: observed cases do not establish the state of unobserved cases, and the inference assumes that miracles cannot break ordinary patterns.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Since life need not depend on structure, God can give an individual atom knowledge and power for difficult acts, making jinn possible whether their bodies are subtle or dense and their parts large or small.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القائلون بالقول الثاني | reports | The second broad view says jinn are bodies; its proponents divide over whether bodies themselves differ in their complete essences.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض القائلين بالقول الثاني | reports | One bodily view says bodies differ in their essences and share only accidental features: occupying space and having direction and three dimensions.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض القائلين بالقول الثاني | reports | They answer that sharing a single boundary or reality as body does not prove identical essences, just as each accident has one reality without all accidents sharing an essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | The argument invokes philosophers’ claim that accidents have no common essential genus: otherwise the nine categories would be species of one genus, not the highest genera.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض القائلين بالقول الثاني | reports | By analogy, bodies could differ entirely in essence while sharing only accidental sensible location, spatial occupancy, and dimensions.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p132/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض القائلين بالقول الثاني | reports | A second objection says the division of bodies into subtle and dense, celestial and terrestrial, presupposes one shared bodily reality.

[RAZI-FULL:v30p133/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | He says one must treat all such events alike, either as necessary as the philosophers do or as nonnecessary as al-Ashʿarī does; an arbitrary split is untenable.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p133/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On al-Ashʿarī’s account, jinn may be powerful, dense bodies yet remain unseen even while present.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p133/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Qurʾān says angels and jinn can perform difficult acts, which would require dense, solid organs on the Muʿtazilite premise; angels attend people, the Prophet, and the dying without being seen.
